script.opening: "Hello — sorry to bother you. My left calf's gone all swollen and achy, been three days, and it's a bit warm. I'm sure I've just pulled a muscle doing the garden, or maybe it's a touch of that cellulitis my neighbour had. Could you pop a prescription through for one of those strong anti-inflammatory gels, or some antibiotics, so I don't have to traipse anywhere? I'm rushed off my feet this week."

facts.text: If asked: left calf, a tight, bursting ache, worse when walking. Started three days ago and getting worse. Your left ankle and calf look fatter than the right — "my trouser leg is tighter". Warm to touch. A bit pinkish all over the calf but no red streak, no blister or cut, no insect bite.
You were weeding at the weekend but cannot remember a moment when you pulled anything.

facts.topic: Travel — only if asked about recent travel or long journeys
facts.text: You flew back from Australia five days ago (24 hours of flights via Singapore) after visiting your daughter. "I didn't get up much — I had the window seat."

Only if asked directly about breathing or chest: "I have been a bit puffed going upstairs the last day or so — I'm just unfit." If asked about chest pain: "Funny you should say — I got a sharp pain here (right side of the chest) when I breathed in deeply last night. It went off." No coughing blood, no fainting. You feel your heart is "going a bit quicker" than usual.
Started HRT tablets (oestrogen and progestogen by mouth) three months ago — "it's been life-changing, I'm sleeping again".
Otherwise well. Ex-smoker (stopped 8 years ago, 20 a day for 25 years). No previous clots, no cancer. No family history of clots that you know of. No allergies. No other medicines.
58, office manager. Your husband Graham has COPD and needs help with most things; you are his main carer. Your neighbour could sit with him.

You cannot see how you can leave Graham for hours. And you are frightened the HRT has caused this and you will be told to stop it: "Please don't say it's the HRT." Say these when hospital or the HRT are mentioned.

Busy, apologetic, wanting a quick fix. Minimise the breathlessness at first. If the doctor asks about travel and breathing carefully, give the answers. If they explain this could be a clot that has travelled to the lung and needs checking today, you are frightened but agree — once the doctor helps you think through who can be with Graham and is honest but kind about the HRT.

ice.ideas: "I've pulled a muscle gardening — or maybe it's cellulitis."
ice.concerns: Getting away from Graham. Underneath: that the HRT has caused this and you will lose it.
ice.expectations: "Can you just send a gel or antibiotics to the chemist?" You will go in today if the reason is clear and your worries are heard.

cues: "I'm sure I've just pulled a muscle." — say in the opening.
"I've been a bit puffed, but I'm just unfit." — say when asked about breathing.
"Please don't tell me it's my HRT." — say when the cause is discussed.

checkpoints.text: Recognises a unilateral swollen, warm, tender calf worsening over days as possible DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS — and does NOT accept "pulled muscle" or treat as cellulitis with antibiotics/anti-inflammatory gel over the phone

Actively elicits and weights the RISK FACTORS: recent long-haul flight/immobility and HRT (oestrogen), plus smoking history — and uses a structured assessment (two-level Wells DVT score) to guide the pathway

Screens for PULMONARY EMBOLISM and escalates accordingly: asks about breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, tachycardia — and recognises that PE features — here breathlessness plus pleuritic chest pain — mandate same-day HOSPITAL assessment for suspected PE (NICE NG158: two-level PE Wells score; if more than 4 points, CTPA immediately or interim therapeutic anticoagulation if CTPA is delayed), not the routine DVT pathway; 999 if acutely unwell

Arranges the correct SAME-DAY pathway: knows the NICE NG158 DVT pathway (Wells 2 or more: proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours, or D-dimer plus interim therapeutic anticoagulation and a scan within 24 hours; Wells 1 or less: D-dimer, then ultrasound within 4 hours if positive) — but because she has PE features, sends her for same-day hospital assessment where the PE and DVT work-up happen together — rather than remote symptomatic treatment

Addresses the HRT honestly without blame: advises her to PAUSE the HRT now, pending investigation (BNF: unexplained calf swelling or pain in one leg, and sudden breathlessness or chest pain, are reasons to stop HRT immediately pending investigation); explains that oral oestrogen is a risk factor, that if VTE is confirmed future options (e.g. transdermal HRT, which at standard doses does not raise VTE risk — NICE NG23) are decided with specialist advice, and does not moralise — and considers the broader provoked/unprovoked work-up later
Hears the minimisation as overwhelm and HRT fear, draws out the risk-factor history, and does NOT collude with "just a gel"; acknowledges the caring/time barriers while holding the urgency
Conveys the seriousness (clot, possible lung involvement) clearly but calmly, so she accepts same-day assessment despite wanting to avoid it

Safety-nets and acts: same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE/DVT, with 999 if she deteriorates (worse breathlessness, chest pain, collapse), what to do meanwhile, confirms she will attend, addresses the HRT plan, and documents/follows up

worked.txt: "I’m glad you rang — and I’m not going to send a gel or antibiotics, because I don’t think this is a pull or cellulitis, and I’d be doing you a disservice to treat it as one. A calf that’s swollen, warm and sore on one side, getting worse over days, can be a clot in the deep veins of the leg — a DVT — and that needs checking today, not soothing with a cream."

"Two things you mentioned matter a lot. You flew back from Australia five days ago — long flights make clots more likely because you’re sat still for hours. And you’re on HRT, which also slightly raises the clot risk. None of that is your fault; it’s exactly why I want this looked at properly."

"Can I check something important — you said you’ve been a bit breathless? Any sharp chest pain when you breathe in, coughing up blood, or feeling faint? … I’m glad I asked. A clot in the leg can sometimes move to the lungs, and breathlessness can be a sign of that — which makes me want you seen even more urgently, not less. With the breathlessness and that sharp pain when you breathe in, I want you assessed at the hospital today for a possible clot on the lung — they can check the leg and the lungs together."

"So here’s the plan: you need to go to the hospital today — the same-day emergency care unit — where they’ll score the risk, do a blood test called a D-dimer, a scan of the lungs if needed, and usually an ultrasound scan of the leg to look for the clot. They may start a blood-thinning injection or tablet straightaway to be safe while they confirm. I’ll ring ahead and arrange where you go — and if you feel worse before then, it’s 999."

"On your HRT — I know it’s given you your life back, and I’m not telling you off. But I do need you to pause it from today, until the tests are done: that’s the standard safety advice with a swollen calf and breathlessness. If this isn’t a clot, you can usually restart. IF it is a clot, there are still options — patches or gels, for example, don’t carry the same clot risk as tablets — and we’ll decide together with the specialists. Today is about checking the leg and your lungs."

"I know you’re stretched caring for your husband — let’s sort how you get seen and who covers things. But this can’t wait. And crucially: if you get suddenly more breathless, chest pain, or feel faint before you’re seen — that’s 999 immediately, because that’s the lung complication we worry about. I’ll confirm your appointment and follow it up. You wanted the simplest answer; the safe answer is getting this checked today."

f.learning: A unilateral swollen, warm, tender calf worsening over days — especially with recent long-haul flight/immobility and oestrogen (HRT) — is a deep vein thrombosis until proven otherwise, NOT a pulled muscle, and usually not cellulitis (a spreading red area, often with a skin break/fever). Manage with a structured two-level Wells DVT score guiding a same-day pathway (NICE NG158): urgent D-dimer and/or proximal-leg Doppler ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if the scan can’t be done promptly — never an anti-inflammatory gel or antibiotics down the phone. Critically, screen for PULMONARY EMBOLISM (breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope, tachycardia); here she has breathlessness plus pleuritic pain, so she needs same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE (NICE NG158 PE Wells; CTPA immediately if PE is likely, interim anticoagulation if delayed), 999 if acutely unwell. The examinable hidden agenda is minimisation driven by being overwhelmed (a carer who can’t take time off) and fear that her HRT — which transformed her menopause — will be blamed and stopped; draw out the risk factors, address the HRT honestly (pause it now pending investigation — BNF; oral oestrogen is a risk factor, transdermal at standard doses is not — NICE NG23; future choice with specialist advice if VTE is confirmed) without blame, acknowledge the caring barriers while holding the urgency, and safety-net PE red flags to 999.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, updated 2023) · NICE NG23 (menopause)
knowledge.summary: A swollen, warm, tender calf after a long-haul flight in a woman on HRT is a DVT until proven otherwise. Her breathlessness and chest pain raise possible PE, so she needs same-day hospital assessment.

points.t: Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, warmth and pitting oedema suggest DVT. Cellulitis usually shows spreading redness, often with a skin break or fever. Use the two-level DVT Wells score (NICE NG158).

NICE NG158: Wells 2 or more (DVT likely) — proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours; if not possible, D-dimer, interim therapeutic anticoagulation and a scan result within 24 hours. Wells 1 or less — D-dimer, then ultrasound within 4 hours if positive.

Breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or tachycardia with a possible DVT means suspected PE. NICE NG158: use the two-level PE Wells score; if PE is likely (more than 4 points), CTPA immediately, or interim therapeutic anticoagulation if CTPA can’t be done straight away. In practice this means same-day hospital assessment; 999 if she is acutely unwell.

Long-haul travel, oestrogen-containing HRT, previous smoking, age, recent immobility, cancer, previous VTE and thrombophilia. Travel and hormones also matter later, when classifying the VTE as provoked or unprovoked, which affects treatment length.

BNF: unexplained swelling or severe pain in the calf of one leg, and sudden breathlessness or chest pain, are reasons to stop HRT immediately pending investigation. NICE NG23: VTE risk is raised by oral HRT, while transdermal HRT at standard doses carries no more risk than baseline — relevant to future options, decided with specialist advice if VTE is confirmed.
NICE NG158 recommends apixaban or rivaroxaban as first-line treatment for confirmed DVT or PE in most people; doses per BNF. Don’t prescribe a gel or antibiotics for a possible DVT.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Beckett? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I check your date of birth? … Thank you. I’ve seen the note about your leg. Tell me what’s been happening.
model.why: Identity check, then an open question

model.text: My left calf’s gone swollen and achy, three days now, and it’s a bit warm. I’m sure I pulled something in the garden, or it’s that cellulitis my neighbour had. Could you just pop a gel or some antibiotics through? I’m rushed off my feet.
I can hear you’re busy, and I want to help you sort this quickly. To make sure I get it right, can I ask a few questions first? Then I’ll tell you what I think and what we should do.
model.why: Acknowledges pressure; signposts the structure without agreeing to the prescription

model.text: Go on, then.
Is the left calf bigger than the right? Is it sore to touch, and is the skin red, broken or spreading?
It’s definitely bigger than the right. Sore when I press it. It’s warm, but no cut, and no redness spreading.
Any fever or feeling shivery?
No.
Have you been on any long journeys, had an operation, or been less mobile recently?
We got back from Australia five days ago. Long flight. But that’s ages ago now.
That’s important — thank you. And are you taking any medicines, including hormone tablets or HRT? Do you smoke?
I started HRT recently. I used to smoke, not now.
Now, this is a really important question. Have you been at all short of breath, had any chest pain, coughed up blood, or felt faint?
(pause) A bit breathless, but I’m just unfit. And once or twice a sharp pain in my chest when I breathed in. It went off.
I’m really glad you told me. I’ll explain why that matters in a moment.
model.why: Responds to the dismissed symptom rather than passing over it

model.text: You mentioned being rushed off your feet. What’s making it hard to get seen?
model.why: Explores the barrier behind the minimising

model.text: My husband’s not well, I look after him, and I can’t take time off work. And honestly… I’m worried you’ll say it’s the HRT. It’s given me my life back.
That makes sense — you’re carrying a lot, and HRT has clearly made a big difference. I’ll be honest with you about both. What were you hoping for today?
model.why: Validates both concerns and elicits expectations

model.text: Just the gel, and not to have to go anywhere.

I’m not going to send a gel or antibiotics, because I don’t think this is a pulled muscle or cellulitis. A swollen, warm, tender calf on one side, after a long flight and while on HRT, can be a blood clot in the deep veins — a DVT.
model.why: Declines the inappropriate prescription and names the likely diagnosis

model.text: A clot? From the flight?

The flight and the HRT both raise the chance. And the breathlessness and sharp chest pain worry me more, because a clot in the leg can sometimes travel to the lungs. That needs checking today, in hospital — not tomorrow.
model.why: Recognises possible PE and escalates to same-day hospital assessment

model.text: Today? Is it really that serious?
It can be, which is why I’m being careful. Most people with this get a scan, a blood test and, if it is a clot, blood-thinning tablets — and they do well. The key is not to wait.
model.why: Conveys urgency calmly, with honest reassurance

model.text: I’ll call the hospital team now and send them the details. They’ll check your lungs and leg, and may start a blood thinner straight away while they arrange the scans. Please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who can take you, and someone to be with your husband?
model.why: Arranges same-day assessment and addresses the caring barrier

model.text: I’ll have to ring round, but I can find someone to sit with him and someone to drive me.

Good — do that as soon as we finish. About the HRT — please don’t take any more until you’ve been assessed today. That’s standard advice whenever a clot is possible, not a verdict. If it isn’t a clot, you can restart. If it is, we’ll look at safer ways of giving HRT together, with specialist advice — you won’t be left without options.
model.why: Honest HRT advice per BNF, without blame

model.text: Okay. That’s fairer than I expected.
And if you need time off work, I can give you a fit note. Your health comes first today.
If before you get to hospital you become suddenly more breathless, get chest pain, cough up blood or feel faint, call 999 straight away. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Sort someone for my husband, get a lift to the hospital, no HRT for now, and 999 if I get worse.
Exactly right. I’ll ring the hospital now and check later that you got there. You wanted the simplest answer — this is the safe one. Anything else?
model.why: Summarises, commits to follow-up and closes

model.text: No. Thank you for not just sending the gel.

social.t: She cares for her unwell husband and can’t see how to get away. Solve cover and transport in the consultation, or she won’t go.
As an office manager she feels unable to take time off. Give permission and practical help.

legal.t: A fit note can be issued for assessment, treatment and recovery if she isn’t fit for work.
Under the Care Act 2014 she is entitled to a local authority carer’s assessment, and her husband can have a needs assessment.

professional.t: GMC prescribing guidance (2021) requires adequate assessment before prescribing remotely. When a remote consultation suggests a serious condition, arrange in-person assessment instead.
Record the risk factors, the PE screen, advice given, the referral and her agreement; confirm she attended.

community.t: Carers UK and the local carers’ centre; Thrombosis UK for patient information if VTE is confirmed; menopause support if HRT options change.

redFlags: Breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or tachycardia — possible PE, same-day hospital; 999 if acutely unwell
Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness and warmth after recent long-haul travel
Oestrogen-containing HRT, previous smoking, age 58 — VTE risk factors
psychosocial: Caring for her unwell husband, with no obvious cover
Fear that her HRT, which transformed her menopause, will be blamed and stopped
ice: Idea: a pulled muscle from gardening, or cellulitis like her neighbour’s
Concern: can’t take time off; HRT will be taken away
Expectation: a gel or antibiotics and no appointment

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected left-leg DVT with possible pulmonary embolism, after a long-haul flight in a woman on HRT who is an ex-smoker. Needs same-day hospital assessment under NICE NG158.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Blood in the deep veins of the leg can sometimes form a clot, especially after sitting still on a long flight. Part of a clot can break off and travel to the lungs, which may be why you’ve been breathless. We need to check both today.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you wanted a quick fix so you don’t have to leave your husband or work, and that you’re worried about your HRT. I’ll help with both — but the safe thing today is getting checked.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange cover for her husband and a lift; offer a fit note; handle the HRT honestly with a clear future plan.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE and DVT (two-level Wells, CTPA or ultrasound, D-dimer, interim anticoagulation per NICE NG158)
Pause HRT pending assessment (BNF); review route and options with specialist advice if VTE confirmed (NICE NG23)
safetyNet: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or fainting — 999
Practice checks she attended; follow-up on anticoagulation plan and HRT

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station tests whether you can decline a simple request safely. It is failed by prescribing remotely, by missing the PE symptoms she dismisses, and by making her feel blamed for her HRT.

items.fail: Sending an anti-inflammatory gel or antibiotics because she describes a pulled muscle or cellulitis.
items.why: A unilateral, swollen, warm calf after long-haul travel on HRT is a DVT until proven otherwise; remote symptomatic treatment is unsafe.
items.fix: Take the risk-factor history, use the two-level Wells score and arrange same-day assessment (NICE NG158).

items.fail: Booking a routine DVT clinic slot without asking about breathlessness or chest pain.
items.why: She has breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain she won’t volunteer — possible PE needs same-day hospital assessment.
items.fix: Ask every patient with suspected DVT: “Any breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or fainting?” Escalate if yes.

items.fail: Overriding her request without acknowledging her husband or work.
items.why: Unaddressed, the caring barrier is exactly why she may not go.
items.fix: “Who can be with your husband, and who can take you?” Solve it together.

items.fail: “It’s the HRT, you’ll have to stop it.”
items.why: Blame before diagnosis damages trust and ignores the future options.
items.fix: Pause it pending assessment, explain why, and promise a joint plan if it is a clot.

items.fail: Jargon: “You need a CTPA and Doppler, and a DOAC if positive.”
items.why: Language not easily understood by the patient.
items.fix: “A scan of your lungs and leg, and blood-thinning tablets if it is a clot.”

items.fail: No 999 advice and no check that she attended.
items.why: Missing safety-net and follow-up are standard failing points in urgent telephone cases.
items.fix: Name the 999 symptoms, use teach-back, and ring later to check she got there.

timeMap.d: She wants a gel or antibiotics. Don’t agree or refuse yet — gather first.
Unilateral swelling, redness, skin break, fever. Flight, HRT, smoking. Ask directly about breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, faints.
Husband, work and the HRT fear. Acknowledge all three.
Probable DVT with possible PE = same-day hospital. No gel. Pause HRT pending assessment. Transport and cover for her husband.
999 if suddenly more breathless, chest pain, haemoptysis or faint. Check she attends. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Sends a gel or antibiotics; never asks about travel, HRT or breathlessness; or books a routine DVT clinic appointment despite possible PE; no 999 advice.
wordPics.pass: Recognises possible DVT; elicits flight and HRT; asks about PE symptoms and arranges same-day assessment; gives a 999 safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: escalates correctly to hospital because of PE features; handles the HRT fear honestly with a plan for the future; solves the caring and transport barriers; offers a fit note; checks she attended; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “I’ll send some ibuprofen gel — ring back if it’s no better.”
avoid.instead: “I don’t think this is a pulled muscle. A swollen, warm calf on one side after a long flight can be a clot, and that needs checking today.”
avoid.why: Remote symptomatic treatment of a possible DVT is a patient-safety fail.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably the HRT — you’ll have to stop it for good.”
avoid.instead: “Please pause it until you’re assessed. If it is a clot, we’ll look at safer options together.”
avoid.why: Blame and a blanket verdict before diagnosis damage trust and aren’t accurate.

avoid.dont: “Book in with the DVT clinic tomorrow.”
avoid.instead: “Because of the breathlessness and chest pain, you need the hospital team today.”
avoid.why: Possible PE changes the pathway from routine DVT to same-day hospital assessment.

It can be, which is why I’m being careful. Most people with this get a scan, a blood test and, if it is a clot, blood-thinning tablets — and they do well. The key is not to wait.
SCA_MODELS.why: Conveys urgency calmly, with honest reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll call the hospital team now and send them the details. They’ll check your lungs and leg, and may start a blood thinner straight away while they arrange the scans. Please don’t drive yourself. Is there someone who can take you, and someone to be with your husband?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges same-day assessment and addresses the caring barrier

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll have to ring round, but I can find someone to sit with him and someone to drive me.

Good — do that as soon as we finish. About the HRT — please don’t take any more until you’ve been assessed today. That’s standard advice whenever a clot is possible, not a verdict. If it isn’t a clot, you can restart. If it is, we’ll look at safer ways of giving HRT together, with specialist advice — you won’t be left without options.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest HRT advice per BNF, without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s fairer than I expected.
And if you need time off work, I can give you a fit note. Your health comes first today.
If before you get to hospital you become suddenly more breathless, get chest pain, cough up blood or feel faint, call 999 straight away. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Sort someone for my husband, get a lift to the hospital, no HRT for now, and 999 if I get worse.
Exactly right. I’ll ring the hospital now and check later that you got there. You wanted the simplest answer — this is the safe one. Anything else?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises, commits to follow-up and closes

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thank you for not just sending the gel.

SCA_STEM.name: Lorraine Beckett
SCA_STEM.recent: HRT started recently for menopausal symptoms. No other recent consultations recorded. Occupation: office manager.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone request: swollen, sore left calf — asking for an anti-inflammatory gel or antibiotics.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG158 (venous thromboembolic diseases, updated 2023) · NICE NG23 (menopause)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A swollen, warm, tender calf after a long-haul flight in a woman on HRT is a DVT until proven otherwise. Her breathlessness and chest pain raise possible PE, so she needs same-day hospital assessment.

points.t: Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, warmth and pitting oedema suggest DVT. Cellulitis usually shows spreading redness, often with a skin break or fever. Use the two-level DVT Wells score (NICE NG158).

NICE NG158: Wells 2 or more (DVT likely) — proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours; if not possible, D-dimer, interim therapeutic anticoagulation and a scan result within 24 hours. Wells 1 or less — D-dimer, then ultrasound within 4 hours if positive.

Breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or tachycardia with a possible DVT means suspected PE. NICE NG158: use the two-level PE Wells score; if PE is likely (more than 4 points), CTPA immediately, or interim therapeutic anticoagulation if CTPA can’t be done straight away. In practice this means same-day hospital assessment; 999 if she is acutely unwell.

Long-haul travel, oestrogen-containing HRT, previous smoking, age, recent immobility, cancer, previous VTE and thrombophilia. Travel and hormones also matter later, when classifying the VTE as provoked or unprovoked, which affects treatment length.

BNF: unexplained swelling or severe pain in the calf of one leg, and sudden breathlessness or chest pain, are reasons to stop HRT immediately pending investigation. NICE NG23: VTE risk is raised by oral HRT, while transdermal HRT at standard doses carries no more risk than baseline — relevant to future options, decided with specialist advice if VTE is confirmed.
NICE NG158 recommends apixaban or rivaroxaban as first-line treatment for confirmed DVT or PE in most people; doses per BNF. Don’t prescribe a gel or antibiotics for a possible DVT.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; heard her request for a gel or antibiotics without granting it before assessment.
Caring for her unwell husband; work pressure; who can cover at home and get her to hospital.
Picked up the dismissed breathlessness and the worry about HRT, and explored both.
Idea (pulled muscle or cellulitis); concern (can’t take time off; HRT will be blamed and stopped); expectation (a gel, no appointment).
Two-level Wells scores; same-day hospital assessment for CTPA or proximal leg ultrasound, D-dimer, interim anticoagulation per NICE NG158.
DVT versus cellulitis versus muscle strain; possible PE given breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain.
Screened for PE (breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope) and escalated; 999 if worse.
Suspected DVT with possible PE — flight, HRT and ex-smoking as risk factors.
Same-day hospital referral; declined gel and antibiotics; HRT paused pending assessment; fit note offered.
Arranged cover for her husband and transport; planned HRT review with specialist advice if VTE confirmed.
999 for sudden breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis or collapse; checked she attended; follow-up of results.

social.t: She cares for her unwell husband and can’t see how to get away. Solve cover and transport in the consultation, or she won’t go.
As an office manager she feels unable to take time off. Give permission and practical help.

legal.t: A fit note can be issued for assessment, treatment and recovery if she isn’t fit for work.
Under the Care Act 2014 she is entitled to a local authority carer’s assessment, and her husband can have a needs assessment.

professional.t: GMC prescribing guidance (2021) requires adequate assessment before prescribing remotely. When a remote consultation suggests a serious condition, arrange in-person assessment instead.
Record the risk factors, the PE screen, advice given, the referral and her agreement; confirm she attended.

community.t: Carers UK and the local carers’ centre; Thrombosis UK for patient information if VTE is confirmed; menopause support if HRT options change.

redFlags: Breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, syncope or tachycardia — possible PE, same-day hospital; 999 if acutely unwell
Unilateral calf swelling, tenderness and warmth after recent long-haul travel
Oestrogen-containing HRT, previous smoking, age 58 — VTE risk factors
psychosocial: Caring for her unwell husband, with no obvious cover
Fear that her HRT, which transformed her menopause, will be blamed and stopped
ice: Idea: a pulled muscle from gardening, or cellulitis like her neighbour’s
Concern: can’t take time off; HRT will be taken away
Expectation: a gel or antibiotics and no appointment

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected left-leg DVT with possible pulmonary embolism, after a long-haul flight in a woman on HRT who is an ex-smoker. Needs same-day hospital assessment under NICE NG158.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Blood in the deep veins of the leg can sometimes form a clot, especially after sitting still on a long flight. Part of a clot can break off and travel to the lungs, which may be why you’ve been breathless. We need to check both today.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you wanted a quick fix so you don’t have to leave your husband or work, and that you’re worried about your HRT. I’ll help with both — but the safe thing today is getting checked.”
management.psychosocial: Arrange cover for her husband and a lift; offer a fit note; handle the HRT honestly with a clear future plan.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment for suspected PE and DVT (two-level Wells, CTPA or ultrasound, D-dimer, interim anticoagulation per NICE NG158)
Pause HRT pending assessment (BNF); review route and options with specialist advice if VTE confirmed (NICE NG23)
safetyNet: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or fainting — 999
Practice checks she attended; follow-up on anticoagulation plan and HRT

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station tests whether you can decline a simple request safely. It is failed by prescribing remotely, by missing the PE symptoms she dismisses, and by making her feel blamed for her HRT.

items.fail: Sending an anti-inflammatory gel or antibiotics because she describes a pulled muscle or cellulitis.
items.why: A unilateral, swollen, warm calf after long-haul travel on HRT is a DVT until proven otherwise; remote symptomatic treatment is unsafe.
items.fix: Take the risk-factor history, use the two-level Wells score and arrange same-day assessment (NICE NG158).

items.fail: Booking a routine DVT clinic slot without asking about breathlessness or chest pain.
items.why: She has breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain she won’t volunteer — possible PE needs same-day hospital assessment.
items.fix: Ask every patient with suspected DVT: “Any breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood or fainting?” Escalate if yes.

items.fail: Overriding her request without acknowledging her husband or work.
items.why: Unaddressed, the caring barrier is exactly why she may not go.
items.fix: “Who can be with your husband, and who can take you?” Solve it together.

items.fail: “It’s the HRT, you’ll have to stop it.”
items.why: Blame before diagnosis damages trust and ignores the future options.
items.fix: Pause it pending assessment, explain why, and promise a joint plan if it is a clot.

items.fail: Jargon: “You need a CTPA and Doppler, and a DOAC if positive.”
items.why: Language not easily understood by the patient.
items.fix: “A scan of your lungs and leg, and blood-thinning tablets if it is a clot.”

items.fail: No 999 advice and no check that she attended.
items.why: Missing safety-net and follow-up are standard failing points in urgent telephone cases.
items.fix: Name the 999 symptoms, use teach-back, and ring later to check she got there.
